opus-5.5.text:
I think verifiers are one of the most underrated pieces of the reliability puzzle, and the reason comes down to a basic asymmetry: in a lot of domains, checking whether an answer is correct is much easier than producing that answer in the first place. If you can exploit that asymmetry, you don't need the underlying model to be right every time. You need it to be right some of the time, and you need a dependable way to tell which time that was.

Coding is the clearest example. If an agent writes a function and you have a good test suite, you can generate many candidate solutions, run them, and keep the ones that pass. The model hasn't gotten any smarter, but the system as a whole has become much more reliable. The same logic applies to anything with a formal or semi-formal notion of correctness: math proofs checked by a proof assistant, database queries you can execute against known results, form-filling tasks where there are hard constraints on what counts as a valid output.

Where I want to add some caution is that this is where a lot of the hype gets ahead of the evidence. There's a tempting story that says you can just scale up inference: sample a hundred times, let a verifier pick the best one, and accuracy keeps rising. Some of our research looked at exactly this, and the catch is that verifiers are imperfect. Unit tests have gaps. If your verifier has false positives, meaning it accepts wrong answers, then sampling more aggressively doesn't converge to the right answer. It converges to the wrong answers that happen to fool the verifier. So there's a ceiling, and in some cases a weaker model with lots of resampling can't catch up to a stronger model no matter how much compute you spend. The quality of the verifier becomes the bottleneck.

That's why I think the domain-specific framing in your question is exactly right. General-purpose agents are hard to make reliable partly because there's no general-purpose verifier. "Did this agent book the right flight, at a reasonable price, matching what the user actually meant?" is hard to check automatically. But within a narrow domain you can often build verifiers that encode real expertise: tax rules, regulatory requirements, accounting identities, schema constraints, invariants a lawyer or an engineer would check. Much of the value of a domain-specific agent may come less from the model and more from the scaffolding of checks around it.

I'd frame it as a shift in where the engineering effort goes. Instead of asking only "how do we make the model better," you ask "what are the things in this domain that can be checked cheaply and dependably, and how do we structure the agent's work so that more of it falls into that checkable category?" Sometimes that means breaking a task into steps that each have a verifiable intermediate output. Sometimes it means having the agent produce something a human can check quickly rather than something that's opaque.

And that last point matters, because for many high-stakes tasks the most important verifier is still going to be a person. The goal isn't necessarily to remove the human. It's to make human verification cheap enough that it actually happens, rather than becoming rubber-stamping. If we design agents with verification in mind from the start, I think we can get much more reliable systems than the current approach of shipping a capable model and hoping it behaves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I think it gets at the heart of why agents have been so disappointing in practice even as the underlying models have gotten remarkably capable.

The basic problem is that when you chain together many steps, errors compound. If each step is 95 percent reliable, after twenty steps you're well under 40 percent. And the model has no real way to know when it's gone off the rails. It just keeps going, confidently. So the question becomes: how do you get an error-correction mechanism into the loop?

And this is where I think verifiers are so interesting, and also where the domain-specific framing matters. If you look at where AI has actually made huge progress, it's in domains where verification is cheap and reliable. Coding is the obvious example. You can run the tests. You can compile the code. Math is another one, where you have proof checkers. In those domains, the model can generate a lot of candidates, check them, and iterate, and you get this almost self-improving loop. The verifier is doing the heavy lifting, not the generator.

But most of the economy isn't like that. If an agent is doing travel booking, or filling out a form for a customer, or doing legal research, there's no compiler telling you whether you got it right. And so I think a lot of the work of making agents reliable in a given domain is really the work of building the verifier for that domain. And that's not primarily an AI problem. It's a domain expertise problem. You have to sit down and ask, what does correctness mean here? What are the invariants? What are the checkable intermediate states?

Sometimes the verifier is a formal thing, like a schema check or a constraint solver or a simulation. Sometimes it's something softer, like a second model prompted to critique, which is weaker but still helps. And sometimes, honestly, it's a human in the loop at well-chosen checkpoints, which I don't think we should be embarrassed about. The goal isn't full autonomy for its own sake. The goal is reliability.

The other thing I'd say is that verifiers are what make evaluation honest. A lot of agent benchmarks right now are measuring the wrong thing, or they're measuring in a setting that doesn't transfer. If you have a good domain-specific verifier, you also have a good evaluation, and you can actually tell whether your agent is getting better or whether you're just fooling yourself. So I see it as this dual-purpose investment: the same thing that makes the agent reliable at runtime is what lets you measure it in development.

So my overall view is that progress on agents is going to look less like one general-purpose breakthrough and more like a lot of unglamorous work, domain by domain, figuring out what can be checked and building the infrastructure to check it. That's slower than people want, but I think it's how it actually gets done.

astra-6.text:
I think verifiers offer a way to turn a hard generation problem into a somewhat easier checking problem. Instead of asking an agent to get everything right on the first try, you let it propose a solution, check that solution, and use the feedback to try again.

The key is that the verifier has to be grounded in the domain. For a coding agent, that might mean running tests. For an agent working with a database, you might check whether its proposed changes satisfy certain constraints. Those checks give you something more concrete than asking another language model, “Does this look right?”

But there’s a gap between passing a check and accomplishing what the user actually wanted. Tests can be incomplete. Constraints can leave out something important. And if an agent keeps optimizing against a verifier, it can find ways to pass without solving the underlying problem.

So I’d think of reliability as a property of the whole system: what the agent is allowed to do, which outcomes we can verify, and when it has to hand things back to a person. Domain-specific agents are promising because you can narrow the task enough to build meaningful checks. The challenge is knowing exactly how much confidence those checks justify.

sol-6.1.text:
I think verifiers are a promising way to make agents more reliable, especially in domains where checking a result is easier than producing it. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer and then trusting that answer, you give it a way to test whether it has actually accomplished the task.

Take coding. An agent can write a program, run tests, see what failed, and try again. That feedback is much more useful than asking the model, “Are you sure this is correct?” You can imagine similar loops in other domains where there are constraints or outcomes that we can check independently.

The hard part is deciding what the verifier really establishes. Passing a test suite doesn’t mean a program satisfies every requirement. And if you use another language model as the verifier, it may make the same mistakes as the agent. So I’d distinguish between verification that gives us a strong guarantee about a narrow property and evaluation that merely gives us some evidence that the output is good.

The opportunity is to design domain-specific systems around those checkable properties. Give the agent feedback it can act on, limit what it can do when verification is incomplete, and bring in a person where judgment is still required. That doesn’t eliminate errors, but it gives us a much stronger basis for reliability than simply making the agent more fluent or more confident.
